title: There Are Microplastics in Coffee. I Tried Two New Brewers That Keep Plastic Out
gist: Microplastic anxiety has spawned a genuinely new premium appliance category: the Simply Good Coffee Plastic-Free Brewer ($480) is the first drip machine with no plastic contact hot or cold, while the Ratio Eight Series 2 ($799) removes plastic only from the hot path (keeping a BPA-free Tritan cold reservoir and polymer frame) and wins decisively on flavor. Wired's reviewer frames the trade-off as materials cost and manufacturing difficulty versus taste and durability, and notes that coffee is a minor microplastic exposure route relative to bottled water, tap water and nylon teabags.

themes.theme: Plastic-free brewing becomes a product category

insights.claim: Nearly every drip coffee maker sold since the first Mr. Coffee machines in the 1970s has included plastic somewhere in the brewing path, making plastic removal a genuine greenfield differentiator in a mature appliance category.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: A commoditized 50-year-old appliance category just found a new axis of differentiation that incumbents built entirely around injection molding are structurally slow to follow.
insights.quote: From the very first Mr. Coffee machines in the 1970s, nearly every drip coffee maker on the market, including many of my favorite drip coffee makers, has included plastic at some point in the brewing process.
insights.locator: Drip coffee is my first true love

insights.claim: Only in the past year have machines shipped that promise to remove plastic from coffee brewing, and just two are named: the Ratio Eight Series 2 at $799 and the Simply Good Coffee Plastic-Free Coffee Brewer at $480.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: The competitive set is currently two SKUs at $480–$799 — early-mover pricing power in a category with essentially no mainstream competition yet.
insights.quote: Luckily, in the past year, a couple new machines have arrived with the promise to remove plastic from the equation
insights.locator: But plastic, as we're now learning, can leach

insights.claim: Simply Good Coffee's plastic-free machine has sold out its production runs more than once since launching last year, turning an obscure value-brand spinoff into a prominent name on demand for plastic-free brewing alone.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Repeat sellouts are the demand signal: consumer microplastic anxiety is now converting into $480 hardware purchases, not just headlines.
insights.quote: it's sold out its production runs more than once since its release last year, riding a wave of interest in plastic-free drip coffee makers
insights.locator: The plastic-free machine rocketed Simply Good

insights.claim: Plastic-free brewers cost significantly more than conventional machines specifically because injection-molded plastic parts are easier to manufacture than stainless steel, borosilicate glass and precision silicone fittings.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: The price premium is a manufacturing-cost floor, not a margin grab — meaning cheap plastic-free drip machines are unlikely near-term and the category stays premium.
insights.quote: Each costs significantly more than machines made with injection-molded plastic parts that are easier to manufacture.
insights.locator: Each promises to deliver delicious, high-end coffee

insights.claim: Tight valves and internal tubing requirements make fully plastic-free automatic drip and home espresso machines expensive and difficult to engineer, which is why the affordable plastic-free options are all manual, low-tech devices.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: The technical barrier sits in fluid-path components — a supplier-level opportunity (glass tubing, food-grade silicone fittings) rather than a brand-level one.
insights.quote: It is expensive and difficult—given the needs for tight valves and internal tubing—to make drip coffee machines and home espresso machines that are entirely plastic-free.
insights.locator: Affordable Plastic-Free Coffee Brewers

insights.claim: Buyers of the fully plastic-free machine are paying for peace of mind rather than cup quality, an explicitly non-performance purchase rationale that reframes the appliance as a health product.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: When the value proposition is anxiety reduction rather than taste, marketing claims and third-party verification — not flavor reviews — become the competitive battleground.
insights.quote: In the end, if you're buying this, you're buying it because, for now, it is the drip coffee maker that is the most dedicated to ensuring that your coffee maker isn't adding microplastics to your cup.
insights.locator: In the end, if you're buying this

themes.theme: Simply Good Coffee: total plastic elimination, flavor cost

insights.claim: The Simply Good Coffee brewer uses a 304 food-grade stainless steel frame with borosilicate glass reservoir, carafe and boiler tube, plus medical-grade sand-based silicone fittings, giving it no plastic contact hot or cold — the only such drip machine the reviewer has tested.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: This is the current benchmark spec any competitor must match to claim 'fully plastic-free' — a concrete bill-of-materials standard for the category.
insights.quote: It is, quite simply, the least plasticky drip coffee machine I am aware of. There's no plastic contact, hot or cold, and very minimal silicone contact.
insights.locator: The frame is made of 304

insights.claim: Simply Good Coffee was founded in 2022 by former Bonavita CEO Laura Sommers and built its business on cheaper takes on premium precision brewers before the plastic-free model made it prominent.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Category disruption came from an ex-incumbent operator repositioning a value clone, not from an incumbent brand — a repeatable pattern for appliance niches.
insights.quote: founded in 2022 by former Bonavita CEO Laura Sommers
insights.locator: Simply Good Coffee is a fairly new name

insights.claim: The Simply Good brewer scores only 7/10 on flavor and 7/10 on ease, with uneven grounds wetting on full 40-ounce batches causing simultaneous under- and over-extraction and a flat cup, so it loses to the Ratio, Moccamaster and Fellow machines on taste.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: A materials-led product can win shelf space while losing on the core performance metric — the durable question is whether health framing outsells cup quality.
insights.quote: And among high-end coffee makers topping $400, Simply Good quite simply does not taste as good.
insights.locator: Most coffee drinkers won't notice these quibbles

insights.claim: The Simply Good machine's always-on warming plate runs during the brew itself, overheating coffee in early phases and adding a measurable 'diner-coffee' oxidation note to every batch even if the carafe is removed immediately.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: A fixable design flaw — a firmware or switch change would close much of the flavor gap, so watch for a revision before writing off the product.
insights.quote: the warming plate gets quite warm, and it stays on during the brewing process, which means the coffee gets overheated during the early phases of brewing
insights.locator: Note that the warming plate gets quite warm

insights.claim: Machining tolerances on the Simply Good brewer are loose — a wobbling showerhead, imperfect fits, and a carafe lid that grinds metal on glass — raising the reviewer's doubts about long-term durability.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Build-quality slippage is the classic tell of a young brand scaling into unexpected demand; warranty claims are the metric to watch.
insights.quote: The lid to the carafe can grind a bit, metal on glass, if you put it on even slightly crookedly—an uncomfortable form of friction that makes me worry about longevity.
insights.locator: Ease of Use and Cleaning

insights.claim: Simply Good's customer service line reached only AI operators during business hours, with a human callback arriving days later — an unresolved support risk offset by a five-year replacement warranty.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: AI-only front-line support is now a reviewable product defect in consumer hardware coverage, a reputational cost of cheap-support substitution.
insights.quote: Calls to the customer service center during business hours reached only AI operators.
insights.locator: Some parts aren't machined as precisely

insights.claim: The Ratio Eight Series 2 never lets hot water or hot coffee touch plastic — borosilicate glass internal tubing, sand-based silicone connectors, stainless steel chassis and brew basket — but is not plastic-free, retaining a BPA-free Tritan copolymer cold reservoir, a polymer frame and BPA-free plastic in the heating element.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Two competing definitions of 'plastic-free' now exist in one category — the labeling ambiguity is where regulatory or marketing-claim risk will surface.
insights.quote: This does not mean it's plastic-free. Its cold-water reservoir is a BPA-free Tritan copolymer.
insights.locator: Aesthetics aside, the Eight's true reason for being

insights.claim: Ratio chose a polymer frame over painted stainless steel deliberately for durability, because steam and moisture degrade painted steel — a case where the plastic-minimizing choice conflicts with the longest-lasting one.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Materials substitution has real engineering costs; brands that go fully metal may trade product lifetime for a marketing claim.
insights.quote: Much of the frame of the Ratio Eight Series 2 is also plastic, a decision made in part for durability: Steam and moisture are actually pretty hard on painted stainless steel.
insights.locator: Plastic Content

insights.claim: The reviewer concedes that the Ratio Eight's plastic exterior fails the aesthetic and emotional test for plastic-avoidant buyers even where it is technically irrelevant to brewing, meaning perceived plastic content can drive purchase decisions independent of leaching risk.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: In anxiety-driven categories, visible material choices matter more than measured exposure — product design should optimize for the perception, not just the physics.
insights.quote: But though it's not relevant to coffee brewing, the Eight's plastic exterior doesn't fully pass the vibes check on a plastic-avoidant brewer.
insights.locator: Plastic Content

insights.claim: The Ratio Eight earns a perfect 10/10 flavor score with exemplary extraction evenness among showerhead brewers, versus 8/10 on plastic-free content and 7/10 on ease of use.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: The taste leader is the compromise product on plastic — buyers must choose one axis, and reviewers will keep splitting recommendations until someone delivers both.
insights.quote: But among showerhead brewers, the evenness of extraction in the Ratio Eight 2 is exemplary, leading to some of the best and most balanced cups I've had this year.
insights.locator: Coffee Flavor

insights.claim: Ratio's flavor advantage comes from deliberately brewing longer than industry norms — up to nine minutes for a full 40-ounce batch with a leisurely bloom, versus about six minutes on the Simply Good machine — plus carefully modulated temperature curves derived from iterative extraction testing.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: The moat is accumulated extraction data and process tuning, not components — hard for a materials-first newcomer to replicate quickly.
insights.quote: Ratio brews a little longer and extracts a bit more fully—as long as nine minutes for a full 40-ounce batch, with a leisurely bloom cycle.
insights.locator: But in some ways, Ratio has moved beyond the SCA

insights.claim: Ratio's flavor engineering transfers down its product line to the cheaper Ratio Six and small-batch Ratio Four, so the taste advantage is available well below the Eight's $799 price.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Ratio has a laddered portfolio the single-SKU plastic-free entrants lack, giving it a wider addressable price band.
insights.quote: This excellent coffee flavor is also evident in the Ratio's other devices, whether the 40-ounce Ratio Six or the small-batch Ratio Four.
insights.locator: Controls are as simple as whispering

insights.claim: The Ratio Eight cannot be cleaned in a dishwasher and requires a specialized tank-cleaning cycle plus Urnex coffee cleaner by hand, an ongoing consumables dependency the stainless-and-glass competitor does not impose.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Recurring cleaner sales are an attach-rate revenue stream, but also a friction point reviewers penalize on ease scores.
insights.quote: Cleaning involves running a cycle with a specialized tank cleaner.
insights.locator: But note that Ratio's parts are not meant for dishwashers

insights.claim: Simply Good obtained independent lab testing showing it holds Specialty Coffee Association 'Golden Cup' parameters — 92 to 96 degrees Celsius, roughly six-minute full batches — but explicitly skipped the more rigorous and expensive SCA certification process.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: 'Tested, not certified' is becoming the cost-saving middle path in appliance credentialing — a claim consumers will need to learn to parse.
insights.quote: But it did not go through the far more rigorous and expensive SCA certification process.
insights.locator: Coffee Flavor

insights.claim: Ratio previously certified all machines to Specialty Coffee Association standards but has now moved beyond SCA parameters based on its own batch-by-batch extraction testing, treating the industry standard as a floor rather than a target.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: When the category leader outgrows the trade standard, certification loses signaling value at the top end and shifts to being a mid-market trust badge.
insights.quote: But in some ways, Ratio has moved beyond the SCA, after testing extractions on batch after batch.
insights.locator: The coffee that arrives from it is also artful

insights.claim: Standard drip machines let brew temperature range wildly through the cycle, which is the mechanism separating premium brewers from commodity ones regardless of plastic content.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Thermal control, not materials, remains the underlying premium-tier moat — a plastic-free machine with poor thermal control still tastes mid-market.
insights.quote: the coffee is going to taste better than most standard drip machines whose temperature can range wildly over the course of the brewing process
insights.locator: This effort places Simply Good squarely

themes.theme: Cheap manual brewers as the volume plastic-free path

insights.claim: The $34 Kalita Wave 185 stainless steel dripper delivers the same flat-bottom even-saturation benefit as the $799 Ratio Eight without plastic, but requires a gooseneck kettle such as the $200 Fellow Stagg EKG to be usable.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: The real all-in cost of the cheap plastic-free route is roughly $234 with the kettle, which narrows the gap to the $480 automatic machine more than the headline price suggests.
insights.quote: Just note that if you're getting into pour-over, you'll need a good gooseneck kettle like the rightfully ubiquitous Fellow Stagg EKG ($200).
insights.locator: A Good Stainless Steel Pour-Over Dripper

insights.claim: Modern French presses commonly use plastic plungers or nylon mesh that wears mechanically and sheds microplastics over time, making a $40 Secura all-stainless press a better plastic-free value than the $110 Yeti or $130 Aarke alternatives.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Mechanical wear sites are the underappreciated leaching vector — a screening heuristic that applies well beyond coffee gear.
insights.quote: A lot of modern French presses use plastic plungers or nylon mesh netting that's likely to sustain wear and leach out microplastics over time.
insights.locator: A Stainless Steel French Press

insights.claim: AeroPress is systematically de-plasticizing a famously plastic product, first with the glass-tube Premium AeroPress and this year with a $170 all-stainless model whose only polymer is a silicone plunger liner in roughly 15 seconds of coffee contact.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: An established brand refitting its core SKU in metal is evidence the plastic-free shift is spreading from startups into incumbent roadmaps.
insights.quote: But the AeroPress was a famously plasticky device for most of its lifespan. Lately, AeroPress is changing this.
insights.locator: A Stainless-Steel Aeropress

themes.theme: Microplastic exposure science and relative risk

insights.claim: A study published last year found that hot-water contact with plastics is the dominant source of microplastic leaching in coffee, which is the technical justification for hot-path-only designs like the Ratio Eight.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: If leaching is heat-driven, the cheaper engineering fix — glass and steel only on the hot side — captures most of the risk reduction, capping willingness to pay for full elimination.
insights.quote: A study published last year showed pretty clearly that hot-water contact with plastics is the main source of microplastic leaching in coffee.
insights.locator: Plastic Content

insights.claim: Prolonged cold-water and light exposure still leaches plastic, as demonstrated by microplastic content in bottled water, so a Tritan cold reservoir holding water for only about ten minutes per brew is a defensible but not risk-free compromise.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Contact-time and temperature are the two variables that determine leaching — a portable screen for evaluating any plastic-contact consumer claim.
insights.quote: But long-term contact with cold water and light can still lead to some leaching, as evidenced by the microplastics content in bottled water.
insights.locator: Plastic Content

insights.claim: Hot coffee carries orders of magnitude fewer microplastics than water bottled in cheap plastic and fewer than tea brewed with nylon teabags, so coffee is likely not a consumer's largest microplastic exposure route.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: The exposure ranking implies bottled water, teabags and tap filtration are far larger addressable markets for microplastic-anxiety products than coffee hardware.
insights.quote: According to a study last year, hot coffee contains orders of magnitude fewer microplastics than water that's been bottled in cheap plastic. It also contains fewer than tea, because of nylon teabags.
insights.locator: What Are the Health Risks From Microplastics in Coffee?

insights.claim: The reviewer redirects plastic-avoidant buyers to a stainless steel water filter before a coffee machine, because tap water may be a bigger exposure source depending on location.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Point-of-use metal water filtration is the higher-leverage adjacent category the coffee story is quietly pointing toward.
insights.quote: Depending where you live, you may have more to fear from your tapwater—and should first look into a good stainless steel water filter.
insights.locator: What Are the Health Risks From Microplastics in Coffee?

insights.claim: The harm mechanism proposed is not chemical reactivity but transport and irritation: microplastics can carry bacteria into the body and, once in the bloodstream, reach vital organs and trigger inflammatory and oxidative responses linked to hormone imbalance, reproductive and nervous system effects, cancer risk, immune weakening and bone weakening.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: The inflammation-mediated harm model, if it holds up in long-term studies, is broad enough to touch food packaging, textiles and water infrastructure — a systemic liability theme, not a niche one.
insights.quote: Plastic is not very chemically reactive. But microplastics can transport other bad things into the body, such as bacteria.
insights.locator: What Are the Health Risks From Microplastics in Coffee?

insights.claim: Long-term human studies on microplastics are not yet in, so the entire premium plastic-free appliance category rests on precautionary consensus rather than established causal evidence of harm from coffee.
insights.speaker: Matthew Korfhage
insights.so_what: Demand here is driven by uncertainty, which cuts both ways: a definitive null result could deflate the category as fast as a positive one would supercharge it.
insights.quote: The general consensus, however, is that we should not welcome any additional tiny plastic particles in our digestive tracts and bloodstream, unless we need to.
insights.locator: What Are the Health Risks From Microplastics in Coffee?
